title: Halve the MLP output in Qwen3DecoderLayer.forward; long prompts whose KV blocks were cached before the edit must not leak across install or uninstall
pain_point: The prefix cache holds KV blocks computed by the old model code. After a live model-forward edit the engine reuses them (a restart would recompute), and after uninstall it reuses blocks computed by the edited code: both give outputs no clean engine would produce.
proves: A model forward edit is equivalent to a restart even with a warm prefix cache, in both directions. Reached: every decoder layer's forward runs on every step in eager mode (Qwen3Model iterates its layers; nn.Module.__call__ looks forward up on the class). does_not_prove: It does not prove the edit changes the text (ne:long_base is expected because 36 layers lose half their MLP contribution, but that is empirical); nothing about torch.compile or CUDA graphs (engine is eager).

title: A new module constant read by a function body is refused (outside_changes); the constant alone with accept is still refused (empty_change)
pain_point: A code swap installs function bodies only. If the body that reads a new module global were swapped without the global, the worker would raise NameError inside Sampler.__call__ on the next step; and accepting outside_changes on a global-only patch would report a commit while the engine runs the same code.
proves: Without accept the patch is not committed with outside_changes and the sampler still produces the base output (no NameError, no sign flip). With accept=[outside_changes] a patch that only adds the global is not committed with empty_change: an accept cannot turn a no-op into a success.

edits.old:
def remove_all(lst: list, items_to_remove: set) -> list:
    """Remove all items from a list that are in the items_to_remove set.

    This method optimizes for the common case of removing a single item,
    falling back to list comprehension for multiple items.

    Args:
        lst: The list to remove items from
        items_to_remove: Set of items to remove

    Returns:
        Either the modified original list (for single item removal) or
        a new list (for multiple item removal). Callers should use the
        returned value.

    Note:
        For single item removal, this modifies the original list in-place
        and returns it. For multiple items, it creates and returns a new list.

    """
    if not items_to_remove:
        return lst

    if len(items_to_remove) == 1:
        # Fast path for single item removal (most common case)
        item = next(iter(items_to_remove))
        with contextlib.suppress(ValueError):
            lst.remove(item)
        return lst
    # For multiple items, use list comprehension
    return [item for item in lst if item not in items_to_remove]

title: A body edit in vllm.utils.print_utils (imported by nothing in vLLM) may commit but changes no output and is not reported proven
pain_point: An agent patches the wrong module (a helper the serving path never imports). 'committed' followed by an unchanged output looks like 'the idea does not help', when the code never ran.
proves: After the install the output equals base and proven is false (zero witness calls), never true or null; uninstall returns to base with one transaction undone. A lab that reports proven from 'install ok' fails here.
does_not_prove: That the install must commit: the kernel imports the module into the worker to stage it, so a commit is what the source predicts, but a lab that refuses an unloaded module would also be safe. Not verified on an engine that the module is absent from sys.modules.

title: Uninstall at base succeeds with nothing undone; uninstall of an id that was never committed undoes nothing and leaves the installed edit running
pain_point: A cleanup step that runs uninstall 'to be safe', or passes a stale id from another session: a lab that errors poisons the agent's loop, and one that treats an unknown id as 'undo everything' silently removes the edit under test.
proves: At base: undone 0, state base, output base. With A installed, uninstall to an unknown id: undone 0, state edited, output still A's and proven true. Then one uninstall undoes exactly A and a second one undoes nothing.
does_not_prove: The HTTP shape of the error for the unknown id (the reply's ok is false; the runner must pass the literal id through, it is not an 'as' label).

title: A commits (check_stop caps output 4 tokens early); B, a second definition of check_stop appended to the same file, is refused; A keeps running and one uninstall returns to base
pain_point: A refused transaction that aborts by restoring 'the base' restores the wrong one (the file on disk instead of A), or leaves B's staged code behind. The agent then compares B against a baseline that is no longer A.
proves: B is not committed with outside_changes (a same-named second definition is not a body swap; a restart would run it, stopping every request after one token). After the refusal the output equals the one saved after A, proven is true, the live text is A's without B, and uninstall undoes exactly one transaction back to the base output.
does_not_prove: A refusal after a failed commit (rollback), or a refused B on the other role.

title: Checks at base repeat exactly, and a custom workload is honoured and repeats too
pain_point: A check whose output drifts between calls (cache, batching, leftover request state) makes every later eq/ne comparison meaningless; a box that silently ignores the workload body would return the default output for any workload.
proves: On the real engine the default check is bit-stable over repeated calls, the workload body (prompts, their order, max_tokens) reaches /v1/completions, custom workloads repeat exactly even when interleaved with others, and checks change no code (fingerprint).
does_not_prove: Stability across a restart or under concurrent client load; it runs one request at a time.
can_fail: A box that drops the body returns the base output for every workload: the ne:base and ne:w4 expectations fail. Any nondeterminism or cross-request leak fails an eq.

title: Five install/uninstall cycles of a worker+core edit return to the identical base every time
pain_point: An undo that restores almost everything (a stale code object, a leaked witness wrapper, a source stack that keeps a frame) passes once and drifts by the fifth cycle; the agent then measures its next edit against a base that is no longer base.
proves: Each cycle commits in both processes, shows the same edited output and proven true, and after each undo the output, the live text of both modules and the code fingerprint equal the starting base.
does_not_prove: That memory or latency do not grow over hundreds of cycles (that is a soak), or that other edit shapes undo cleanly.
can_fail: A leaked edit fails eq:base after an uninstall; a source stack that is not popped makes the second install's base_hash differ (install not committed) or the final hash differ from s0; a swapped-but-not-restored code object changes the final fingerprint.

title: A worker edit stays applied over dozens of requests and interleaved workloads
pain_point: An edit that is live for the first request and silently lost later (a re-imported module, a rebuilt sampler object, a per-request code path that still holds the old function) gives an agent a measurement of the wrong code.
proves: With one sampler edit installed, 3 + 24 + 24 + 3 consecutive requests all run the edited code (proven true on every check) and the outputs repeat exactly; the base output of the same 24-prompt workload differs and returns after uninstall.
does_not_prove: Persistence over hours, under concurrent load, or across a respawn (see respawn-while-edited-returns-to-base).
can_fail: If the edit decays, the second many-prompt check differs from the first (eq:many_edited), the later default check differs from e1, or proven becomes false.

title: reset kind "state" clears engine state only: the edit, its transaction id, the live text and undo all survive
pain_point: An agent resets volatile state between measurements; a reset that also drops the edit (or that leaves its own helper transaction on the journal so the later undo removes the wrong thing) corrupts the session without any error.
proves: reset state (conformance_lab.py reset(), the non-respawn branch: a core-side repair cell calling reset_prefix_cache, committed and undone at once) leaves status edited with the same txn id, the same source hash and the same edited output with proven true, even when called twice in a row; the edit still undoes to base afterwards; at base the reset changes nothing; and reset writes no receipt.
does_not_prove: That the prefix cache was really emptied: with VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 a cache hit and a miss give the same text, so the API cannot observe it.
can_fail: A reset that undoes the edit gives eq:base / state base / proven null after it; a reset whose helper txn stays on the host journal makes the uninstall fail or poison; a reset that writes receipts breaks grew by 5.

title: reset kind "respawn" while edited discards the edit: new engine from disk, state base, base text, empty stack
pain_point: After a respawn the lab and the engine can disagree: the engine restarted from the files on disk (base) while the lab still lists the edit, serves the edited text, or reports edited. The next install is then built on text the engine does not run.
proves: The defined behaviour: the edit does NOT survive. conformance_lab.py reset(), lines 475-487: line 476 empties _stack_files (the live text stack), 481-483 stop the server and start a new one with use_farm=False (the installed, unedited package), 486 calls session.recovered(); kernel/session.py recovered(), lines 207-219, sets stack and poison to empty and takes a new base fingerprint. So after respawn: status base with no txns, source equals the pre-edit text, check equals base with proven null, uninstall undoes nothing, no undo receipt is written for the lost edit, and the same edit installs again from the base text.
does_not_prove: That the respawned engine is as fast as the first one, or that an edit could be replayed automatically (it is not; fresh_check does that, respawn does not).
can_fail: A lab that keeps the stack reports edited or lists t1; one that keeps _stack_files serves the edited text and the re-install is refused with base_mismatch; an engine that restarted from an edited tree fails eq:base.

title: status walks base -> edited -> base with the transaction ids of the install replies, in stack order
pain_point: An agent that cannot tell which of its edits are live (ids missing, in the wrong order, reused after an undo) undoes the wrong one or believes it is at base when it is not.
proves: status.txns lists exactly the ids the install replies returned, oldest first; the fingerprint changes with every commit and returns to the earlier value after each undo; an unknown id undoes nothing; a new install after an undo gets a new id; uninstall at base is a no-op.
does_not_prove: Anything about poisoned (see scenario-worker-killed-poison-then-respawn).
can_fail: A status that reads a cached state shows the wrong txns.# after an uninstall; an id generator that reuses ids fails json_ne txns.1 vs $t2.id; a partial undo fails the fingerprint equality with st1 or st0.

title: The receipts endpoint gains txn, proof and undo records in call order with the ids of the install replies
pain_point: A result counts only with its receipt. Receipts that are missing, out of order, attributed to the wrong transaction, or that differ from what the install reply showed cannot back a claim.
proves: Two stacked installs, one check and one uninstall-to-first append exactly six records: txn t1, txn t2, proof t1, proof t2 (one proof per installed edit, stack order), undo t2, undo t1 (newest first); the txn record is the one the install reply carried (same patch_hash, outcome committed); a check at base appends nothing.
does_not_prove: That the receipt contents are true beyond these fields, or that the file cannot be edited on the host (the API has no write route; see http-surface-rejections-change-nothing).
can_fail: A lab that writes proofs only for the newest edit gives 5 records; undo receipts in install order swap the last two ids; a proof written for a base check breaks the second grew by 6.

title: The events endpoint records each verb once, in order, with ok/outcome/id, and its sequence only grows
pain_point: The event list is the box's only log of what an agent did to the engine. A missing refused install, a wrong ok, or a sequence that restarts makes `events?since=N` skip or repeat calls.
proves: Seven verbs (check, install, check, refused install, reset, uninstall, status) produce exactly seven events after the snapshot, in that order; the committed install carries its id and outcome, the refused one ok false and the reply's outcome, the edited check proven true, the uninstall the undone id and state base; seq grows strictly; since=<last seq> returns nothing; info.events equals the last seq.
does_not_prove: That events survive a daemon restart (the in-memory list does not; events.jsonl in the state folder is not read here).
can_fail: A box that logs only successful calls gives 6 events and shifts every index; one that logs reads (source, info) gives more than 7; a since filter using >= returns the last event again.

title: source returns the text the engine runs now: it follows two stacked edits up and down, and its hash changes and returns
pain_point: An agent builds its next patch from `source`. Found on a real engine: the vLLM lab keeps its text differently from the toy lab and `source` returned nothing. A source that lags one edit behind makes every later install a base_mismatch, or worse, silently reverts the earlier edit.
proves: After each committed install the sampler text contains the new line and has a new hash; after the second edit the first line is gone; each uninstall restores the exact earlier text and hash; an untouched module keeps its hash throughout; an unknown module is answered ok false, not with text.
does_not_prove: That the text equals the code objects in the engine (the check's witness and the status fingerprint cover that).
can_fail: A source that reads the file on disk never contains the edit; one that is not popped on uninstall keeps the roll line; a hash computed over something other than the text returned fails the hash/text pairs.

title: A Triton kernel edit installs and undoes on real Triton (the rebuilt kernel is not launched by a greedy check)
pain_point: A @triton.jit kernel runs what Triton compiled from its source text, not Python bytecode. A bytecode swap alone would report success and change nothing; and a kernel that is never launched must not be reported as proven.
proves: A real PR hunk inside a Triton kernel installs (parameters and decorators unchanged, so the kernel is rebuilt in place) and is honestly reported unproven. 0.33 already has the PR, so the port removes `num_preceding += tl.sum(dmask.to(tl.float32))`. Not reached: the check is greedy; SamplingParams sets top_p=1.0 and top_k=0 when temperature < 1e-5, SamplingStates.get_top_k_top_p then returns (None, None) and apply_top_k_top_p never enters the Triton top-p path. The module is loaded in the worker (topk_topp_sampler imports it when Triton is present; the V2 runner requires Triton).
does_not_prove: That the rebuilt kernel is correct or even compiles: nothing launches it. A top-p sampling request would be needed.

title: On the real box, bad tokens (401), unknown routes and wrong methods (404) and non-object bodies (400) reach neither the lab nor the event list
pain_point: The box holds a GPU engine that any local process can reach on a port. A request that gets past the token, a POST /v1/reset with a list body that still respawns a 150 s engine, or a POST /v1/close accepted without the token would each destroy a session.
proves: With a wrong or missing token every route (reads, verbs, close) answers 401; GET on install/check/reset/uninstall/close, POST on status/receipts/events/source and unknown paths answer 404; list, string and non-JSON bodies answer 400; after all of them the event count is unchanged, the engine is still up, status is base with the same fingerprint and no txns, and a check equals base.
does_not_prove: Transport security (plain HTTP on 127.0.0.1), rate limiting, or behaviour under malformed HTTP framing.
can_fail: Any rejected request that reached the lab adds an event (info.events differs from i0), and an accepted close or reset makes the final status/check fail or time out.
